summary: Recommends that authors writing IANA Considerations sections consider assigning a small range of numbers for experimentation and testing. People experimenting with protocols often need a protocol number or constant, even in closed environments. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3692 recommends reserving numbers that people can use to test protocol ideas. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) assigned two Internet Protocol (IP) values for tests; they are shared, not guaranteed unique, and should not be enabled by default.

subtitle: Set aside protocol numbers for experiments rather than reusing temporary assignments.

tldr.problem: Protocol experiments may need a number, but temporary assignments can be hard to reclaim and unsafe to reuse after they appear in products.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends reserving a small range for experimentation. Experimental features in products must be disabled by default and explicitly enabled by the user.
tldr.outcome: IANA assigned IP protocol values 253 and 254 for testing. RFC 3692 is BCP 82 and updates RFC 2434.

today: RFC 3692 is Best Current Practice 82 and updates RFC 2434. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 3692.

sections.title: Why Experiments Need Protocol Numbers
sections.content:
A protocol extension may need a number or constant so two systems can recognize it during testing. Getting a permanent assignment can require review, and temporary assignments can be difficult to reclaim when an experiment ends.

If a temporary value is built into a product, it may be unclear whether reuse would affect deployed devices. The RFC therefore recommends a range reserved specifically for testing rather than a temporary loan of a normal value.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing a protocol idea can require a number that identifies it. A temporary assignment can be difficult to take back, so a reserved testing range is easier to manage.

sections.title: How Experimental Values Are Used
sections.content:
Devices that agree to take part in an experiment may use an experimental value for their test. Other implementations may use the same value for a different experiment, so the value is not guaranteed to be unique outside the test environment.

Experimental values are not for general deployment and must not be enabled by default in products. A user must explicitly enable the feature and, in most cases, configure which value to use. A successful experiment can later seek a permanent value through normal procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Two groups may use the same test number for different purposes. A product must leave experimental behavior off until a user chooses to enable and configure it.

sections.title: Reserving Values in Protocol Documents
sections.content:
Protocol authors should consider reserving a small set of experimental values in an IANA Considerations section. The useful size depends on the protocol; if different value ranges trigger different behavior, more than one test value may be needed.

Values reserved for experiments must never become permanent assignments. Products that include the feature must require explicit configuration, including reprogramming when the product has no user interface.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol authors can specify a small testing range when they define an allocation. Products must require a deliberate configuration choice before using an experimental value.

sections.title: IP Protocol Numbers for Testing
sections.content:
IANA assigned IP Protocol field values 253 and 254 for experimentation and testing. They come from the upper end of the number space so they stand out from existing assignments.

Other name spaces can reserve experimental values through a published RFC or, where appropriate, IESG Approval. The RFC updates the guidelines in RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC sets aside IP protocol values 253 and 254 for tests. Other registries can use their normal allocation processes to define experimental values.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The RFC states that it has no known security implications. It warns that enabling an experimental value by default can cause interoperability problems when another experiment uses the same value, which is why products must keep the feature disabled by default.

RFC 3692 is Best Current Practice 82 and updates RFC 2434. The batch metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes RFC 3692.
sections.plainLanguage: The document identifies no known security implications, but shared test values can conflict. RFC 3692 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2434.
